parole.significato: nominal suffix (ending) of the first declension of the nouns.
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Indo-European *-os.

Related to Old Church Slavonic гъ (gŭ, “comparative particle used in негъли (negŭli, “than”)”), of unclear further origin. Beekes derives the particle from Proto-Indo-European *gʰo ~ *gʰe (discourse particle).

parole.significato: forms nouns with the meaning "place to put something" (normally animals)
parole.testo: Ambrazas links this suffix to dė́ti (“put”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁-.

parole.significato: forms adjectives with the meaning "of", "made from" or "pertaining to" the original noun
parole.testo: Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *-iHnos. Cognate with Latvian -ains, Old Church Slavonic -ьнъ (-ĭnŭ). Compare -inas.

parole.significato: Adjectival suffix, applied to verbal and nominal roots to denote a disposal or tendency towards something
parole.testo: Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *-ós (“adjectival ending”). Pairs such as lañkas (“bend”) : lankùs (“flexible”) find parallels in Sanskrit रुधिर (rúdhira-, “blood”) : रुधिर (rudhirá-, “red”), Ancient Greek δόλιχος (dólikhos, “a long run”) : δολιχός (dolikhós, “long”) and suggest that oxytone str

parole.significato: Used to form the past adverbial (padalyvis) participle
parole.testo: From Proto-Indo-European *-wṓs. Cognate with Proto-Slavic *-vъ. See also -usi.
The most convincing explanation derives this word from Proto-Indo-European *h₁edʰ-, *h₁odʰ- (“pointed, sharp”), as with eglė (“spruce, fir”) < *ed-li, see for more. Compare Latvian adît (“to darn”).

parole.significato: to defenestrate, throw out of a window
parole.testo: Probably from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eydʰ- (“to ignite”). Cognate with Ancient Greek αἴθω (aíthō, “id”).
Probably ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eidʰ-.

An adverb formed on the basis of Proto-Indo-European *h₂olyos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂el- (intriguingly, however, this word is not discussed by Derksen). For the suffix, compare visái (“entirely”). Related to Proto-Celtic *olyos (“all”) and, with a different suffix, Proto-Germanic *allaz (“all”

Cognate with Latvian elks, Gothic 𐌰𐌻𐌷𐍃 (alhs, “temple”). The generally accepted etymology derives this from Proto-Indo-European *h₂lek- (“to protect”), but it could very well be from a non-IE substrate language.

Cognate with Latvian mūžs (“life”), Old Prussian amsis, amsin (“people”), with further origin unclear: * King derives the Baltic terms from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ems-ǵʰ-, an extension of *h₂ems- (“to give birth, beget”), comparing Hittite 𒄩𒀭𒍝𒀸𒊭𒀸 (ḫa-an-za-aš-ša-aš, “offspring”) in particular. Inherited from Old Lithuanian añt, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂en-t. Compare Sudovian an.

Probably related to añt (“on”), or to Proto-Indo-European *h₂entíos, Proto-Indo-European *h₂ent-. Alternatively, related to Armenian անութ (anutʻ, “armpit”), via a Proto-Indo-European *h₂(V)nt-h₂-o-. Cognate with Latvian azuote (“bosom”).
From Proto-Indo-European *h₂en- (“grandmother”). Cognates include Old Prussian ane, Ancient Greek ἀννίς (annís), Old Armenian հան (han).
From Proto-Indo-European *h₁epi, *h₁opi.

From Proto-Indo-European *h₁epi, *h₁opi. Cognate with Latvian ap (“around, about”), Old Prussian ep- eb-, ab-, English by, Latin ob, Irish ar, Sanskrit अपि (ápi, “also, further, even”), Albanian mbi, Ancient Greek ἐπί (epí, “on, at, by”), Armenian և (ew).

parole.significato: eagle owl (primarily the Eurasian eagle-owl (Bubo bubo) and the long-eared owl (Asio otus))
parole.testo: Phonetically matches Proto-Slavic *ȍpakъ (“the other way round”), Sanskrit अपाक (ápāka-, “distant”), अपाका (apākā́, “far, behind”), Old Norse ǫfugr (“turned the wrong way”), which are from Proto-Indo-European *h₂epo-h₃kʷ-, from *h₂epó (“behind”) + *h₃ekʷ- (“eye”). From Proto-Balto-Slavic *apwalus. Morphologically from ap- + valus, the latter part of which may be from Proto-Indo-European *welH- (“to turn, wind”). Cognate with Latvian apaļš (“round”), and further related to Proto-Slavic *obьlъ (“oval”), which contains the zero-grade of the root.
Cognate with Proto-Slavic *obora (“string, twine”). Related to verti (“to pierce, string”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wer- (“to cover, shut”).

From Proto-Indo-European *h₂er- (“thus, so”), thought to be a specialized conjunctional usage of the Proto-Indo-European root's usual "to fit" meaning. Cognate with Latvian ar (“whether, if, with”), Ancient Greek ἄρα (ára, “then”).

From Proto-Indo-European *h₂er-t-i, from *h₂er- (“to fit”). The Lithuanian form is probably an old locative; compare dialectal artiẽ and namiẽ (“at home”). Exact cognates include Ancient Greek ἄρτι (árti, “just, just now”), Old Armenian արդ (ard, “just now”). For the meaning, compare Ancient Greek ἄ
Neologism introduced by Lithuanian linguists in the early 20th century, of unclear formation logic. Perhaps created off a hypothetical Proto-Indo-European *h₁es-men-, from *h₁es- (“to be”).
From Proto-Indo-European *h₂éh₂usom, *h₂ews- (“dawn; gold”). Cognate with Old Prussian ausis (“gold”), Latin aurum (“gold”), Tocharian A wäs (“gold”), Tocharian B yasā (“gold”).
From Proto-Indo-European *h₂ewg- (“to increase”). Cognate with Latvian aûgsts (“high”), Old Prussian *aukt(a)s, Latin augustus (“exalted, lofty”). Doublet of Augustas.
From Proto-Indo-European *h₂ew- (“to weave”). Compare Latvian aust (“to weave”), Sanskrit वयति (váyati).
From Proto-Indo-European *h₂ew-iǵʰ- Cognate with Latvian àuzas (“oats”), Old Prussian wyse (“oats”), Proto-Slavic *ovьsъ (“oats”), Latin avena.
Inherited from Proto-Indo-European *bʰéy(h₂)-dʰh₁-e-ti, from *bʰeyh₂- (“to fear”). Cognate with Latvian baĩdît (“to frighten, scare”), Old Prussian pobaiint (“frighten”).
From the root bai- + -lė (see baidyti), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeyh₂- (“to fear”). Cognate with Latvian baîle (“fear”).

parole.significato: April (fourth month of the Gregorian calendar)
parole.testo: Traditionally derived from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- (“white”), perhaps via an unattested formation *balandis galambis (“white-marked pigeon”) (for the latter, see Latin columbus (“male dove”)). The "April" meaning is apparently from a meaning of "having a white or bare patch" (whether this refers
From Old Lithuanian balgnas (“saddle”), cognate to (possibly borrowed from) Old Prussian balgnan (“saddle”). The term is thought to be ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰelǵʰ- (“to swell”).
Derived from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewdʰ-. Related to busti (“to wake up”), baudyti (“incite, instigate”).
Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewd- (“to beat”). Cognate with Latvian bel̂zt (“to strike”).
From Proto-Indo-European *bʰendʰ-ros (“tied (to someone)”), from *bʰendʰ- (“to bond”). Among the word's cognates, compare in particular Ancient Greek πενθερός (pentherós, “father-in-law”).
From Proto-Indo-European *bʰer-n-o-, from *bʰer- (“to bear”). Synchronically equivalent to ber̃ti + -nas. Cognate with Latvian bȩ̄̀rns (“child”), Proto-Germanic *barną (“child”).
From Proto-Indo-European *bʰl̥d-. Cognate with Latvian bil̂dêt (“to speak, say, address, answer”), Swedish bulta (“to knock”).
From Proto-Indo-European *bʰleyǵ- (“to shine”)
From Proto-Indo-European *bʰrewH-. Cognate with Old Prussian brewinnimai (“we help”), Proto-Germanic *breutaną.
Possibly from Proto-Indo-European *brewn-; see also English preen, Albanian brez.
From Proto-Indo-European *bʰrend-. Cognate with Latvian briêst (“to swell, ripen, mature”), Old Prussian pobrendints (“made more difficult”), Old Irish do·eprinn (“to flow, trickle”).

Has been compared with: * Proto-Slavic *bъtъ, *bъtvo (“spout, scion”), Proto-Germanic *buddǭ (“bud”) from Proto-Indo-European *bʰew- (“to swell, to blow”); * Proto-Germanic *putōną (“to push”), presumably from Proto-Indo-European *bud- (“to spout”) (perhaps of substrate origin).
From Proto-Indo-European *bus- (“to kiss”), see also Latin bāsium (“kiss”), Albanian buzë (“mouth”), Persian بوسیدن (bôsidan, “to kiss”)).
From Proto-Indo-European *bʰerH-o-s, a form of *bʰerH-. Cognate with Latvian bȩ̃rs (“bay”).
Nominal formation from bū̃dytis (“to exercise, practice”), from būd-, the lengthened zero-grade of Proto-Indo-European *bʰewdʰ- (“to be aware, alert”).

From Proto-Indo-European *dolgʰ-. Cognate with Latvian dalgs (“scythe”), Old Prussian doalgis (“scythe”) and possibly Proto-Slavic *dolga (“splint”). Further related to Old Norse telgja (“to cut, carve”) and Catalan dalla (“scythe”).

Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *delh₁- (“to split, divide”). Cognate with Latvian dalis (“part, share”), as well as dalià (“fate”) and dalỹkas (“thing, matter”). Possibly related to dailyti (“to divide”) and thence to Proto-Slavic *dělъ (“part”) (from *děliti (“to divide”).

From Proto-Indo-European *delh₁- (“to split”). Cognate with Latvian dalît (“to divide, share”), Old Prussian dellieis (“(imperative 2nd singular) share!”), Proto-Slavic *odolě̀ti (“to overcome, defeat”).
From Proto-Indo-European *dʰor-éyeti, an iterative formation of *dʰer- (“to support, hold”). Cognate with Sanskrit धारयति (dhārayati, “hold”), Latvian darīt; see the Latvian for other theories.

Cognate with Latvian dārzs, with further origin outside of Baltic uncertain. Smoczynski suggests a derivation from dir̃žas (“belt”), which he tentatively derives from Proto-Indo-European *derǵʰ- (“fenced lot”); one possible cognate is Proto-Germanic *targǭ (“edge, rim, border”) (whence English targe

Traditionally derived from Proto-Indo-European *deǵʰ- (“liquid, mixture”) and compared with Old Irish deug (“drink, draught, potion”), Welsh diod (“id”); the zero-grade of this root is perhaps found in žuvi̇̀s (“fish”) < *dǵʰ-uH-. From Proto-Indo-European *nébʰos (“cloud”). Cognates include Latvian debess (“sky”), Polish niebo (“sky, heaven”), and Ancient Greek νέφος (néphos, “cloud, mass of clouds”).

parole.significato: to spoil, waste, scorn, scold (dialectal, Old Lithuanian)
parole.testo: From Proto-Indo-European *dʰerg-. Cognate with Latvian der̂dzêtiês (“to quarrel, fight”), Old Prussian dergē (“hate”) 3pl., Middle High German terken, derken (“to make dark, soil, defile”).
From Proto-Indo-European *dʰer- (“to hold”). Cognates include Sanskrit धरति (dhárati) and Latin firmus. See also Lithuanian darna (“harmony”).
From Proto-Indo-European *deḱs-. Cognate with Proto-Slavic *desnъ, Sanskrit दक्षिण (dakšiṇa), Ancient Greek δεξιός (dexiós), Latin dexter.

Derived from di̇̀dis (“big, large”) + -elis, with further etymology of the first component uncertain. Possibly from Proto-Indo-European *deyh₂-dʰe-, from *deyh₂- (“to shine”), with semantic shift "shining" > "visible" > "large"; in this case, related to Homeric Greek δέατο (déato, “[he/she/it] showe
From Proto-Indo-European *dʰeygʷ- (“to stick, to plant”). Cognate with Proto-Slavic *děgati, *dьgna, Proto-Germanic *dīkaz (“pool, puddle”), Latin fīgō (“pierce, pin, fasten, fix”).
From Proto-Indo-European *dayh₂wḗr. Cognate with Russian де́верь (déverʹ), Sanskrit देवर (devara).
From Proto-Indo-European *dʰelg-, *dʰelk- (“to stick, prick, stab”), see also dilgus (“prickly”), Latin falx (“hook, sickle”), Old Irish delg (“spine, needle”).
From Proto-Indo-European *dʰr̥Hbʰ-, a zero-grade of *(s)dʰerHbʰ- (“to exert force”). Cognate with Latvian dir̂bt (“to walk fast”), Proto-Germanic *derbaną (“to work”).
Causative of di̇̀rgti (< Proto-Indo-European *drHǵʰ-). Cognate with Russian дёргать (djórgatʹ, “to tug”) and Dutch tergen (“to provoke”).

Of unclear origin. Smoczyński tentatively derives the word from Proto-Indo-European *derǵʰ-; compare dar̃žas (“vegetable garden”), as well as possibly Proto-Germanic *targǭ (“edge, rim, border”) (whence English target). Compare also Polish dzierżyć (“to hold”), itself from Proto-Slavic *dьržati (“to
From an earlier deverbal adjective *dóvas, from Proto-Indo-European *deh₃-wo-s, from *deh₃- (“to give”). Cognate with Latvian dâvana (“gift”).
From Proto-Indo-European *dʰrebʰ- (“to fracture”). Cognate with Latvian drebēt; also see Proto-Slavic *droba (“crumb”).

From Proto-Indo-European *dʰrews-k-eh₂-, from *dʰrews- (“to break into pieces”), which appears to be related to Proto-Indo-European *dʰrā́ks (“dregs, sediment”). Cognate with Latvian druska (“crumbs”), Old Prussian dmskins (“earwax”); outside of Baltic, compare Proto-Germanic *drōhsnō (“dregs”), Wel

parole.significato: to dare, to have the courage.
parole.testo: From Proto-Indo-European *dʰers- (“to dare”).
Singular forms are used dialectally: Samogitian duja (“mist”), Dzūkijan duja (“ashy earth”). From the same root as dū́mai (“smoke”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewh₂- (“smoke, mist”).
Cognate with Latvian dvaša (“breath”). For the root see dvė̃sti (“breathe, blow”), daũsos (“air”), Proto-Indo-European *dʰwes-.
A k-extension to the same Proto-Indo-European root *dʰweH- as dūmas (“smoke”), dūlis (“thick smoke”), dvasia (“spirit, breath”). Compare notably dvelkti (“blow, smell, waft”).

parole.significato: to look, to stare, to watch for
parole.testo: Cognate with Latvian dairîties (“to stare, to gaze”) (o-grade), Old Prussian endyrītwei (“to look at”), and likely Proto-Slavic *diriti (“to seek, to look for”) (whence Bulgarian ди́ря (dírja, “to look for”)). The Balto-Slavic forms are perhaps further derived from Proto-Indo-European *deyH-r (“to e

From Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁-l-, from *dʰeh₁(y)- (“to suckle, nurse”). Cognate with Latvian dêle (“leech”), Ancient Greek θηλή (thēlḗ, “breast, teat”), Latin fēllō (“to suck”), Albanian dele (“sheep, ewe”).
A reflexive verbal formation from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewgʰ- (“to produce, be strong”); related to daũg (“much, many”).
Unclear. Has been compared with Proto-Balto-Slavic *algā́ˀ, itself from Proto-Indo-European *h₂elgʷʰ-éh₂-, though it's semantically problematic. Cognate with Latvian elgtiês.
Possibly from Proto-Indo-European *h₁er-.

From gadinti (“to spoil”) + orą (“air”). The first element is from Proto-Indo-European *g(ʷ)edʰ- (“to smell”); for the second element compare aušra (“daybreak”). See also Avestan 𐬔𐬀𐬌𐬧𐬙𐬌 (gaⁱṇti, “stench”), 𐬛𐬎𐬲𐬔𐬀𐬌𐬧𐬙𐬌 (dužgaⁱṇti, “smelling badly”), Sogdian 𐼲𐼻𐽂 (ɣnt, “stench”), Persian گند (gand, “sten

Cognate with Latvian gàiss (“air, atmosphere, sky”); further origin outside of Baltic uncertain. Of unclear origin. According to Derksen, from a Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰen- (“to flourish, swell; enough, numerous”), which he appears to consider the same as *gʷʰen- (“to strike, slay”) (whence giñti (“drive, chase”)), perhaps via semantic shifts "slay" > "booty (from spoils of war)" > "flourish".
From Proto-Indo-European *gʷerH- (“to praise”). Cognate with Latvian gãrbe (“cautious treatment”), Lithuanian ger̃bti (“to honor”).
From Proto-Indo-European *gerh₂-.
Ultimately of imitative origin, from Proto-Indo-European *geH- (“to sing, cry”), related to Proto-Slavic *gajati (“to croak, caw”).
Perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *geybʰ- (“to skew, to crook, to split”), cognate with Latvian gìbt (“to subside, to sink”), Proto-Germanic *kībaną (“to quarrel”).
Related to girti (“to praise”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷerH- (“to welcome, greet, praise”), or garėti (“to evaporate”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰer- (“warm, hot”).
From Proto-Indo-European *gʷerH- (“to praise”). Cognate with Old Prussian gērbt (“to speak”), and further related to Latvian garbât (“to care for, attend”), Lithuanian garbė̃ (“honor”).

From Proto-Indo-European *g(ʷ)edʰ- (“to smell”), see also Avestan 𐬔𐬀𐬌𐬧𐬙𐬌 (gaⁱṇti, “stench”), 𐬛𐬎𐬲𐬔𐬀𐬌𐬧𐬙𐬌 (dužgaⁱṇti, “smelling badly”), Sogdian 𐼲𐼻𐽂 (ɣnt, “stench”), Persian گند (gand, “stench”). Compare the first element of gadinti orą (“to fart”).

From Proto-Indo-European *(s)gʷes-. Cognates include Ancient Greek σβέννῡμι (sbénnūmi, “to extinguish”), Sanskrit जासयति (jāsáyati, “to exhaust”), Irish bás (“death”), and Polish gasić (“to extinguish”).

From Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰh₂eyd-ro-, from *gʷʰh₂eyd- whence also Ancient Greek φαιδρός (phaidrós, “bright, beaming”) and perhaps gai̇̃sas (“gleam, ray”). Within Baltic, related to Latvian dzidrs, Lithuanian gaidrus.
From Proto-Indo-European *gʷelh₂-. Cognate with Latvian zīle, Old Prussian gile, Polish żołądź, Greek βάλανος (válanos), and Latin glāns.

parole.significato: kvass (a fermented cereal-based low alcoholic beverage, often flavored with fruit, honey and herbs.)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Lithuanian girà, from the zero-grade root of the verb gérti (“to drink”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷr̥h₃-, zero-grade of the root *gʷerh₃- (“to swallow, devour, eat”). Cognate with Samogitian gėra (“kvass”), Latvian dzira (“liquid food for feeding livestock, beverage, alcoholic

Perhaps from a Proto-Indo-European *gʷerdʰ- (“to sound”), which appears to be related to *gʷerH- (“to praise, recite”); the suffix *dʰ- may be from *dʰeh₁- (“to do, put, place”). Cognate with Latvian dzirdēt; outside of Baltic, compare especially Old Armenian կարդամ (kardam, “to shout, call”).

parole.significato: to creak, to squeak, to crunch
parole.testo: From imitative Proto-Indo-European *gerh₂- (“to cry hoarsely”), see also Proto-Slavic *grakъ.
From Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰeh₂- (“to yawn, gape”). Related to Proto-Germanic *gōmô, *gaumô (English gum, German Gaumen, Icelandic gómur).

Along with griū́ti (“to collapse”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrewH- (“to rush in, attack”). Cognate with Latvian graût (“to destroy, thunder”), Latin ingruō (“to attack”), Ancient Greek χράω (khráō, “to attack, inflict”). The "destroy" and "thunder" meanings are traditionally treated separately in

Probably from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrey- (“to smear, paint, streak”) (which Derksen reconstructs as *ǵʰrey(H)-), and cognate with Ancient Greek χρῑ́ω (khrī́ō, “to smear, anoint”). However, the details of the word's phonetic development are unclear, due to the existence of related forms with kr- ins

Along with griáuti (“to destroy, demolish”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrewH- (“to rush in, attack”). Cognate with Latvian grût (“to collapse, rush”), Latin ingruō (“to attack”), Ancient Greek χράω (khráō, “to attack, inflict”).

From a zero-grade stem of Proto-Indo-European *gʰrewbʰ-. LEW suggests a relation to Old High German grob (“thick, strong”) and Proto-Slavic *grǫbъ (“coarse; rude”), from *gru(m)b- (with nasal infix). Cognate with Latvian grubulis.

parole.significato: lie, lie down (assume a lying position to rest)
parole.testo: Cognate with Latvian gul̃t (“go to bed”). Related to guolis (“lair, den”) (see there for more cognates). Derksen connects this etymon with dialectal gvaldýti (“cram, pack”), gvãlis (“lair, den”), which means the -u- must go back to Proto-Indo-European *-u̯-. The root may therefore be Proto-Indo-Euro

Perhaps from a Proto-Indo-European *gwel- (“dwelling-place, hole”), and cognate with Latvian guōļa (“nest, lair”). Outside of Baltic, compare Old Armenian կաղաղ (kałał, “hole, hiding-place”) and perhaps Ancient Greek γωλεός (gōleós, “hole”).
From Proto-Indo-European *gew- (“to curve, to slither”) or a related root. Potentially cognate with Old Armenian կուռն (kuṙn, “back”).

Probably from Proto-Indo-European *gʷewH- (“to defecate”). Cognate with Old Prussian gīdan (“shame, disgrace”), as well as perhaps Proto-Slavic *gadъ (“creepy creature”), Proto-West Germanic *kwād (“evil”), Proto-Slavic *govьno (“crap, turd”).
From Proto-Indo-European *gʷelH-eh₂, from *gʷelH- (“to throw, sting, hurt”); see also the verb dzelt (“to sting”).
From Proto-Indo-European *h₂erH-, also reconstructed *Her-. Cognate with Latvian irt (“to disintegrate, crumble”) and Proto-Slavic *oriti.
From Proto-Indo-European *h₁r̥h₁-yé-ti (“to row”).
From Proto-Indo-European *eḱs (“out of”), *eǵʰs, *h₁eǵʰs. Cognates include Ancient Greek ἐξ (ex), Latin ex, Old Irish ess-, a, ass (Irish as) and Old Church Slavonic из (iz).
Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *yewg- (“to yoke, harness, join”). Compare Ancient Greek ζεύγνυμι (zeúgnumi, “to joke”) and Latin iungō (“to join”).

From Proto-Indo-European *Hyéh₂-kos (“that, who, which”). The negative meaning of the Lithuanian term comes from an earlier *nijóks (“neither”), with the negative prefix (from Proto-Balto-Slavic *nei) being later dropped.
From Proto-Indo-European *yunégti ~ *yungénti. Cognates include Latvian jūgt, Sanskrit युङ्क्ते (yuṅkte, “to yoke”), Ancient Greek ζεύγνυμι (zeúgnumi) and Latin iungō (whence English join).

Durative formation from a root kib-, cognate with Latvian kabināt (“to hang, hook”) and Old Prussian kabīuns (“hung”), seemingly from a Proto-Indo-European *(s)kebʰ- (“to hook, bend, fasten”), though cognates in other branches are unclear. From Proto-Indo-European *kʷod.

According to Pokorny, from Proto-Indo-European *ked- (“to fume, smoke”), comparable to Proto-Slavic *kaditi (“to burn incense”), Proto-Indo-Iranian *kádruš (“tan, brown”), Ancient Greek κέδρος (kédros, “cedar”). However, these words are all of uncertain origin. Compare Latvian kadiķis.
Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *keHy- (whence also English heat, hot).

Cognate with Latvian kakt (“to come to an end”), of uncertain further origin. Smoczynski, following Stang, derives the words from a Proto-Indo-European *kʷek-, comparing Proto-Slavic *čekati (“to wait, expect”) as the only adduced cognate. This is favored by Derksen. Cognate to Latvian pirkt; further origin outside of Baltic uncertain. Perhaps from a Proto-Indo-European *prek-, from *per-k-, a hypothetical -k-variant of *perh₂- (“to sell”), in which case compare Ancient Greek πέρνημι (pérnēmi, “to sell”).

From Proto-Indo-European *p(y)eh₂w- (“to strike, hit”) (traditionally reconstructed as *paw-); cognate with Latvian pļaũt (“to mow, reap”), Latin paviō (“to beat, strike”), Ancient Greek πταίω (ptaíō, “to nudge, crash into”), Tocharian B pyakar (“they struck down”), Old English fȳran (“to castrate”)

From Proto-Indo-European *plewk- (“to flow; to flap, splash”), extended form of the root *plew-. Cognate with English fly and flee. Related to Latvian pliens, Old Prussian playnis, with further origin outside of Baltic uncertain. From Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂-no-, from *pleh₂- (“flat”). Cognate with Latvian plā̂ns (“flat, even, thin, weak”); outside of Baltic, compare especially Latin plānus (“level, flat”).

Like Etymology 1, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂- (“flat”). Cognate with Latvian plā̃ns (“floor, threshing floor”), Old Prussian plonis (“threshing floor”); outside of Baltic, compare especially Old Norse flórr (“floor of a cowshed”).
Per Smoczyński, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *(s)peh₂- (“to draw, to pound”). Possibly akin to Proto-Slavic *patriti (“to perceive, observe”).

Cognate with Latvian pràts (“mind, intellect”), Old Prussian prātin (“counsel”). Plausibly related to Proto-Germanic *frōdaz (“wise, cautious”), Latin pretium (“price”), from Proto-Indo-European *pret- (“to understand, interpret”). Cf. pràsti (“to acquire a habit, understand”), and see Latvian prast

Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂peh₃lH-, a compound of *h₂epó (“off, away”) + *h₃elh₁- (“to fall”). Cognate with Latvian pult (“to fall (obsolete)”), Old Prussian aupallai (“finds”); outside of Baltic, compare Proto-Germanic *fallaną (“to fall”) (whence English fall), Ancient Greek ᾰ̓πόλλῡμῐ
From Proto-Indo-European *pod-óm (“vessel”). Cognate with Latvian pods (“pot”), Old Prussian podalis (“id”); outside of Baltic, cognate with Proto-Germanic *fatą (“vessel, container”).
From Proto-Indo-European *poḱ-éye-ti, the causative of *peḱ- (“joyful; pretty”).
From an uncertain Proto-Indo-European root shared with Albanian purth (“diarrhea”) and Latvian pùrvs (“swamp”), which see for more.
From Proto-Indo-European *pewḱ- (“pine”). Cognate with Old Prussian peuse (“pine”) and Sudovian puse (“pine”).
Derived from Proto-Indo-European *ped- (“to walk, step”). Cognate with Latvian pēkšņs (“sudden, abrupt”), Proto-Slavic *pěšь (“pedestrian; on foot”).
Related to Lithuanian rišti (“bind, tie”), from Proto-Indo-European *wreyḱ-.
Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rem- (“to rest”). Compare Latvian rāms (“calm, tranquil”).

From Proto-Indo-European *wrongʰ-eye-ti, from *wrengʰ- (“to twist, squeeze”); cognate with Proto-Germanic *wringaną (“to wring”). The Proto-Slavic *orǫga (and possibly *rǫgati) may share the same origin.
From Proto-Indo-European *Hrót-o-s (“wheel”). Cognate with Latvian rats (“wheel, cart”), Sanskrit रथ (ratha, “two-wheeled war chariot”), Latin rota (“wheel”), Old High German rad.

parole.significato: to mean, signify, convey indicate, express
parole.testo: Related to ryškùs (“clear, bright, distinct”), rýkšti (“to make clearer and brighter”), as well as Old Church Slavonic рѣснота (rěsnota, “reality, truth”). From Proto-Indo-European *h₃rḗǵs, cognate to Old Prussian rikīs, Latin rex, German Reich, Irish rí, English rich.

From Proto-Indo-European *r̥k-, zero-grade root of *rek-. Related to rikdýti and full-grade rė̃kti. Cognates include Old Czech řéci (“to say”) (1sg. řku), Old Polish rcy (“say”, imperative), Old Church Slavonic рьци (rĭci, “id”).
From rimti (“to be quiet”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rem-.
Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rem- (“to rest”).

Of uncertain origin, with two competing theories: * From Proto-Indo-European *writ-e-ti (“to twist, roll up”), and related to riẽsti (“to bend, curve, warp”). Derived from rẽtas (“thin, rare”). Possibly related to Latin rēte n (“net”), conceivably from Proto-Indo-European *ret-.
Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rewg- (“to retch, vomit, puke”), see also Old English rocettan (“to burp”). Compare Latvian rūgts (“bitter”).
Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *swé (“self”). Within Baltic, cognate with Latvian savs, Latgalian sovs, Lithuanian svetimas, Lithuanian svečias.
From Proto-Indo-European *sekʷ- (“to say”).

From Proto-Indo-European *semH- (“to scoop, draw”). Cognate with Latin sentīna (“bilgewater, bilge (of a ship)”), Proto-Celtic *semeti (“to pour”), and possibly Ancient Greek ᾰ̓́μη (ắmē, “shovel; pail”).
From Proto-Indo-European *sénos (“old”). Cognate with sẽnas, Latin senex.

From Proto-Indo-European *seyk- (“to reach (for)”), and cognate with Ancient Greek ῑ̔́κω (hī́kō, “to come, reach”). The acute form in the common variant of the Lithuanian (which also has an expected circumflex form siẽkti), is difficult to explain, however.
From Proto-Indo-European *si-né-h₂-ti ~ si-n-h₂-énti (“to bind, fetter”). Cognate with Latvian siet (“to bind, tie”).
Unclear. One theory connects this to Proto-Germanic *slēpaną (“sleep”), from Proto-Indo-European *sleh₁b- (“to be weak”).

parole.significato: to be ill, to suffer from
parole.testo: From Proto-Indo-European *swergʰ- (“to worry, care for”), with loss of the *-w-. Cognate with Latvian sìrgt (“to be ill”).

A denominal verb from an unattested *skala or *skalas (compare i̇̀šskalos (“water with which a vessel is rinsed”)), from the same word family as skélti (“to split, cleave”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelH- (“to cut, to cleave”). Cognate with Latvian skalināt (“to rinse”); see skal̃bti (“to wash”)

From Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelH- (“to split”).

Perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *skend- (“to jump, dart, climb, scale, scan”), with semantic shift "jump, dart" > "jump into water" > "plunge into water" > "sink, drown". If so, then cognate with Latin scandō (“to climb, ascend”); see there for more cognates.
From Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelH- (“to split”). Related to Latvian šķilvis.
From Proto-Indo-European *skn̥H-, the zero-grade of *skenH- (“to tear off”); cognate with Latvian šķĩt (“to pluck leaves; to clear bushes”), Proto-Germanic *skinþą (“skin, hide, peel”).
According to Būga and Otkupščikov, linked to sklim̃bas (“slice of bread”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kel- (“to cut”).
In ablaut with skelė́ti (“to owe”), from Proto-Indo-European *skel- (“to owe”). Cognate with Proto-Germanic *skulaną (“to owe”).
Adjectival formation from the lengthened o-grade of Proto-Indo-European *skel- (“to owe, be guilty”). See also skolà (“debt”) and skõlinti (“to lend, owe”), from the same ablaut grade.

Cognate with Latvian skriet (“to go, run, fly”), seemingly from a Proto-Indo-European *(s)krey- (“to turn”), and related to Proto-Slavic *krīdlò (“wing”), as well as Proto-Balto-Slavic *kréiwas (“crooked”); see the latter for more.

Probably from Proto-Indo-European *ksweybʰ- (“to shake”). Cognate with Latvian skubrs (“hasty”), as well as dialectal Lithuanian skubrùs (“lively”); outside of Baltic, possibly related to Proto-Germanic *skeubaną (“to push, drive”), Proto-Slavic *skuti (“to pluck”), Sanskrit क्षुभ् (kṣubh, “to shake
Probably from Proto-Indo-European *k⁽ʷ⁾sewbʰ- (“to shake”); see skubùs (“urgent, hurried”) for more.
From Proto-Indo-European *(s)kerd- (“to move, sway, swing, jump”), see also Old High German scerdo (“hinge”), Latin cardō (“hinge”), Lithuanian kárti (“to hang”).
Adjectival formation from Proto-Indo-European *h₃sleydʰ- (“to slip, slide, be slippery”). Cognate with Latvian slids (“slippery”); see also slýsti (“to slip, slide, glide”).

Cognate with Latvian slēpt, of uncertain further origin. Traditionally derived from Proto-Indo-European *(s)klep- (“to steal”), with dissimilative loss of the *-k- from the *skl-, and cognate with Tocharian B kälyp- (“id”), Ancient Greek κλέπτω (kléptō, “id”). From Proto-Indo-European *melh₂- (“to grind, crush”) with s-mobile, see also Latvian smalks (“fine”), Lithuanian smėlis (“sand”), Latvian smelkne (“fine flour”), Latvian smiltis (“sand”), Latvian smilkts (“sand”), Proto-Slavic *mělь. The -k- remains unexplained, but could have been inserted for ease
From Proto-Indo-European *melh₂- (“to mill, grind”), similar to malti (“to grind”).
Perhaps from a Proto-Indo-European *snop-; compare English snap, Proto-Germanic *snabulaz (“muzzle, mouth”).

parole.significato: October (tenth month of the Gregorian calendar)
parole.testo: Cognate with Latvian spaļi (“waste of flax or hemp”), Old Prussian spelanxtis (“splinter”); outside of Baltic, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pelH- (“to split, tear off”). If so, then compare Ancient Greek σπολᾰ́ς (spolắs, “leather garment”), Latin spolium (“skin, hide; spoils”), Old Church Sl
Related to spáusti (“to press, squeeze”), spūdà (“pressure”), from Proto-Indo-European *spewd-.
From Proto-Indo-European *spewd- (“to press, hurry”). Cognate with Ancient Greek σπεύδω (speúdō, “to press on, hasten”).

From Proto-Indo-European *pstḗn (“teat, nipple”). Compare Proto-Germanic *spenô (“nipple”), Ancient Greek στήνιον (stḗnion, “breast, chest”), Persian پستان (pestân, “breast”), Sanskrit स्तन (stána, “female breast, nipple”), Tocharian B päścane (“pair of breasts”).

parole.significato: to explode, to blow up, to shatter
parole.testo: Cognate with Latvian sprâgt (“to burst, to blast”). Perhaps from a g-extension of Proto-Indo-European *(s)perH- (“to trample, to spurn”) > *sprh₂eg- (“to crack, to bust”), akin to Proto-Slavic *pьrga (“pollen, bloom”), Proto-Germanic *sprekaną (“to speak”), Ancient Greek σφρᾱγῑ́ς (sphrāgī́s, “seal”)
Derived from srė̃bti (“to slurp”), from Proto-Indo-European *srebʰ- (“to sip, gulp”).

From Old Lithuanian substantive root *srāv- < *srōw-, hence also Lithuanian sravė́ti; ultimately from the present stem of Proto-Indo-European *srew- (“to flow, stream”). Cognate with Latvian strā̀va, Ancient Greek ῥοή (rhoḗ), Sanskrit स्रव (srava).

parole.significato: to flow, to stream, to run (for fluid)
parole.testo: From Proto-Indo-European *srew- (“to flow”), related to Proto-Slavic *strujiti (“to gush, to flow”). Per Derksen, probably of secondary origin with metatonic acute (in contrast to the circumflex in Lithuanian sravė́ti (“to flow”), sravà (“bleeding”), sraujà (“jet, flow”)).
From Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- (“to stand”). Cognate with Latvian statît (“to place”), Old Prussian preistattinnimai; also related to Ancient Greek στατός (statós, “standing”), Latin status.

From Proto-Indo-European *stebʰ-h₁-yé-ti, the essive present of *stebʰ- (“to stand still, harden; prop up, support; pole”). By synchronic analysis, an iterative formation of stèbti (“to be amazed, astonished”), itself from the above root. The sense development is "to stand still" > "to be amazed" >
From Proto-Indo-European *steyb-, see also Old Armenian ստէպ (stēp, “speed, haste”) and Lithuanian staibus (“courageous, strong”). Compare Latvian stiprs.

From Proto-Indo-European *strel-, *strēl-, from *ster- (“line, streak, stripe; jet, spurt; beam”). Cognates include Latvian strēle, Old Church Slavonic стрѣла (strěla), Russian стрела́ (strelá), Ukrainian стріла́ (strilá), Czech střela, Polish strzała.

From Proto-Indo-European *sewh₁-leh₂, from *sewh₁- (“to press”). Direct cognates include Latvian sula (“juice, sap”), Old Prussian sulo (“curdled milk”), Proto-Indo-Iranian *súraH (“intoxicating liquor”).

parole.testo: su- (“co-”) + prasti (“to acquire a habit or inclination”), the latter from Proto-Indo-European *pret- (“to understand”).
Cognate with Latvian svainis (“brother-in-law”), from Proto-Indo-European *swoy-n(i)o-s, a derivative of *swe- (“self”).

parole.significato: to have a dream, to hope, to wish, to desire
parole.testo: Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)weh₁-. Akin to Proto-Slavic *xvějati (“to sway, tremble”), English sway, Sanskrit स्वजते (svájate, “he embraces”).

Probably from Proto-Indo-European *su-ey-kas, from *h₁su- (“good”) and *ey-, *h₁ey- (“to go”); the original meaning would then have been “one who goes or walks well”, whence “healthy” and then “unharmed.” For other theories, see Latvian sveiks (“safe”).
From Proto-Indo-European *swer- (“heavy, hanging”); cognate with Proto-Germanic *swēraz (“heavy; serious”).

From Proto-Indo-European *sēy- (“syrup, mead”), akin to dialectal Bulgarian се́я (séja, “to suckle”), Polish soić (“to breastfeed”). Possibly further related to Proto-Germanic *saimaz (“mead, honey”) (whence Norwegian seimr, German Seim).
Related to sèkti (“to follow”), from Proto-Indo-European *sekʷ- (“to follow”).

From Proto-Indo-European *ter- (“soft, tender, young”).

Related to the verb tikė́ti (“to believe”). Cognate with Latvian tikrs (“good, sound”). Could be also cognate to Proto-Indo-European *-teros (“especially such”), with maybe epenthetic /k/ similarly to that as in krikštas (“baptism”) (from Old Church Slavonic крьстъ (krĭstŭ)).
Probably from Proto-Indo-European *tenk- (“to be suitable”), and cognate with Proto-Germanic *þinhaną (“to thrive”).

From Proto-Indo-European *tlh₂-tó-m (“lifted up”), from *telh₂- (“to bear, tolerate”). Derksen connects Sanskrit तीर्थ (tīrtha, “passage, ford”) as an exact cognate; however, the Sanskrit term is generally thought to derive from *terh₂- (“to cross, pass through”) instead. Related to Russian толь (tolʹ) and Latin tālis. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *tó-.

parole.testo: From Proto-Indo-European *olbʰ-. Compare Old Armenian ողբ (ołb).

From Proto-Indo-European *Heh₃s-y-os (compare Welsh onnen, Latin ornus (“wild mountain ash”), Proto-Germanic *askaz, Russian я́сень (jásenʹ, “ash”), Albanian ah (“beech”), Ancient Greek ὀξύα (oxúa, “beech”), Old Armenian հացի (hacʻi)).
From Proto-Indo-European *h₁óh₃s (“mouth”). Compare Latvian õsta, Proto-Slavic *ūstà (“lips, mouth”).

Cognate with Latvian uosvis (“father-in-law”), from Proto-Indo-European *ṓ-pḱu-iyos (“having livestock”). The *ṓ is akin to the आ- (ā-) in Sanskrit आमनस् (ā́-manas, “having turned one's mind to”), while the *-pḱu- is the zero grade of *péḱu (“livestock”).
From Proto-Indo-European *lewH- (“louse”), see also Sanskrit यूका (yūkā).
Derived from veikti (“to do, to work, to move”), from Proto-Indo-European *weyk- (“to contain, to envelop”, “to yield”, “to overcome”). See also Proto-Slavic *čelově̀kъ (“man”).
Related to vỹkti (“go”), vei̇̃kti (“do, act”), vaikýti (“chase”) + -(i)oti (“verb suffix”). From Proto-Indo-European *weyk- (“overcome”).
From the same root as vei̇̃sti (“to breed, rear”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *weys- (“to raise, produce”). Cognate with Old Prussian wẽisin (“fruit”), Old Norse vísir (“bud, sprout”).
From an earlier *vaid-tas, interpreted as "knowledge (regarding diseases and how to treat them)", from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- (“to know, see”). Cognate with Old Prussian waist (“to know”).
From Proto-Indo-European *ul (“the tail”), Cognate with Latin *ulos (“tail”) (attested in adūlor), Sanskrit वाल (vā́la, “tail”), Proto-Slavic *volsъ (“hair”).

From Proto-Indo-European *word-. Compare with Latvian var̂de, Old Armenian գորտ (gort).

From Proto-Indo-European *werǵʰ- (“bind, wind together”), see also veržiù (“to fence in, string”), Old Norse virgill (“snare”), Proto-Germanic *wurgijaną (“to strangle”).

parole.significato: to go by vehicle, drive, ride
parole.testo: Perhaps a denominative, from važas (“wagon, carriage”) + -iuoti. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *weǵʰ- (“to bring, transport”).
